title: Comparative Characterization of Extracellular Vesicle-Enriched Fractions from Fresh Salivary Gland Secretions and Lyophilized Head Tissue of Hirudo nipponia
content: Extracellular vesicles (EVs), as endogenous mediators of intercellular communication, have been extensively characterized in mammalian systems; however, EVs from non-mammalian medicinal organisms remain comparatively undercharacterized. Despite the well-established medicinal value of the invertebrate H. nipponia—largely attributed to the complex bioactive secretions of its salivary glands—the characterization of its salivary gland-derived extracellular vesicles has yet to be fully explored, with current studies still in the nascent stages. In this study, four types of extracellular vesicles were isolated from the salivary glands of living H. nipponia and the heads of lyophilized H. nipponia using differential ultracentrifugation. Their morphological features and particle size distributions were characterized via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), respectively. Finally, their protein compositions were comprehensively analyzed using proteomic techniques. Characterization by TEM and NTA confirmed that microvesicles (MVs) and exosomes (EXOs) from both origins displayed classical saucer-like vesicular structures, with diameters consistently ranging from 100 to 300 nm. Notably, proteomic analysis indicated that EVs harvested from live H. nipponia salivary glands preserved a broader profile of proteins with reported pharmacological activities than the LP-derived preparations. In conclusion, the successful isolation and profiling of H. nipponia salivary gland-derived EVs provide a foundational framework and fresh perspectives for exploring the biological roles of extracellular vesicles in invertebrates.
